name: French Guiana
summary_text: French Guiana stands under the national framework of France. Identity documents, the criminal code, anti-discrimination law and marriage law operate here as in metropolitan France, with no separate local statute on gender identity.  French law does not criminalise trans status or gender expression. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791, retained in the Penal Code of 1810, and that position extends to French Guiana.  Legal gender recognition has been available since 1 January 2017 under the law of 18 November 2016. Change of gender marker requires an application to a court and is granted without surgery, sterilisation, psychiatric certificate or medical diagnosis. Change of first name is handled separately at the registry office.  Discrimination on the ground of sexual identity has been prohibited since July 2012. The term in Penal Code article 225-1 was replaced by gender identity on 18 November 2016. The Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, training or employment and discriminatory sanctions or dismissal on the ground of gender identity.  Since 2017 transphobia constitutes an aggravating circumstance for any crime punishable by imprisonment under French law applicable in French Guiana.  Trans women in France whose detention placement follows legal gender face a legal gray area in prison allocation. The national preventive mechanism found in its opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations persist in French places of deprivation of liberty. Both findings apply in French Guiana as a jurisdiction applying French detention law.  Gender-affirming surgery performed in France was legalised in 1979. Specialised trans healthcare in French Guiana remains limited by remoteness, with extended waiting times and inequitable access by location reported at national level in a 2022 ILGA-Europe report.  One overview of French Guiana reported societal transphobia and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting.  Police-identified victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in France numbered around 1,380 in 2018 and around 1,870 in 2019, a rise of 36 percent reported on 16 May 2020.  Same-sex marriage has been legal in all overseas departments and territories including French Guiana since the 2013 marriage-equality law, following civil solidarity pacts available since 1999. Pride events are held in French Guiana. One travel guide rated French Guiana Very Safe for LGBTQ+ visitors and described a small scene anchored in Cayenne with no listed venues.  Conversion therapy is banned under the law published on 1 February 2022, following Senate passage on 7 December 2020 and National Assembly concurrence on 25 January 2022. The offence carries two years imprisonment and a fine of 30,000 euros.

name: Guam
summary_text: Guam stands under the United States framework as an unincorporated territory of the United States. Federal hate crime protection for gender identity has applied in Guam since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.  Same-sex marriage has been lawful in Guam since June 2015. Chief Judge Frances M. Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the prohibition on 5 June 2015 in a case brought after Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero were denied a licence in April 2015, with the ruling effective at 8 a.m. on 9 June 2015. Licences were issued four days after the ruling, and the Guam Marriage Equality Act of 2015, passed on 11 August 2015, made marriage laws gender neutral. The ruling cited Latta v. Otter.  Airport screening in Guam follows Transportation Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. Body scanner and pat down procedures can disclose a transgender traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request alternative screening and may escalate problems on the spot. Guidance addresses pre flight packing and document and screening mismatches, and most transgender travellers pass screening without incident.  Guam is described as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment. That description is framed for LGBTQ people generally rather than for transgender people specifically.

sources.title: Pennington v. Government - Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals
sources.documents: Only reported sodomy case in Guam in early 1950s; victory for defendant on procedural grounds that trial court lacked authority to try without jury
sources.detail: Cited in History section as 'Pennington v. Government'; no URL visible in text
